slides.say: Basket A contains five hundred eggs, and basket B contains six hundred eggs. How many eggs must be moved from basket A to basket B, so that basket A will contain nine thirteenths of the number of eggs in basket B?
So eggs move from A to B, and after the move, A should have nine thirteenths of what B has. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, with an equation, and then by plugging in the answers.
Let's put the numbers in order, before and after. Before the move, A has five hundred and B has six hundred. We don't know how many eggs we move, so let's call that number x.
After the move, A has lost x eggs, so it has five hundred minus x. And those same x eggs went into B, so B has six hundred plus x.
Now the condition. A after the move is nine thirteenths of B after the move. So five hundred minus x equals nine thirteenths, times the bracket six hundred plus x.

slides.say: To get rid of the fraction, we multiply both sides by thirteen. Thirteen times the bracket five hundred minus x, equals nine times the bracket six hundred plus x.

slides.say: Open the brackets. Thirteen times five hundred is six thousand five hundred, and thirteen times x is thirteen x. Nine times six hundred is five thousand four hundred, and nine times x is nine x.

Now we add thirteen x to both sides, and take five thousand four hundred off both sides. Six thousand five hundred minus five thousand four hundred is one thousand one hundred. And nine x plus thirteen x is twenty-two x.

Instead of dividing by twenty-two in one go, let's divide both sides by eleven first. That gives a hundred equals two x, so x is fifty. We move fifty eggs, and choice number two is our answer. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
